'Sir

'You cannot but wonder you haue not hard from Mr Hoby or from mee before this but I thought wee should haue benn in London before this but my husband and my sonn both haue benn ill, my sonn was so ill that it put us in greate feare what the Issuent would bee, ye small pox wee fered but I thanke god it was not and both Mr Hoby and my sonn are resnable well and Mr. Hoby gonn to London yester day but I suppose hee may forgett to speake with you therfore I thought good to let you know formerly Mr Hoby did send mee to Mr Rylie (or Reyly) and hee told mee, that Mr Hoby might giue Sir Edward Hobys Armes with a barr, with out any charge or leaue from your office, if so then Mr Hoby doth hope that Sir Edward Bissh will not Aske much for to lett him giue it that way which you spake ofe which is ye better way Soe I doe desier to know of you this, whether Mr Hoby may giue Sir Edward Hoby his Fathers Armes with ye Barr with out any Charge or leaue from your office, and next what Sir Edward Bish and your office must haue, to haue leaue to giue Thes Armes as you mentioned which is ye best way. Sir Edward did giue a very fine Crest which I believe hee did purchace, for formerly I finde they gaue an nother and Mr Hoby hath that patten for ye new Crest now in ye hous, which I doe Intend to bring to London yer long, but you told me sumthing must be donn now, before the tearme but if it could hansomly be deferred till I could come to London which will be aboue a fortnight hence then I could know Mr Hobys minde and let you know it, but if that cannot be pray let me know as soone as you can whether Mr Hoby may giue the Hobys armes with out leaue from your office (and also our Children) or whether it must be purchased, and if so what the charge will bee, that so wee may know what to doe and giue you an Ansur directly, Sir this is all att present from

Your freind and servant
Kat: Hoby'

Eng. lett. c. 328, fol. 599r (with seal and postal marks) Oriell College: May the 17th Sir. I received your letter by Mr Brace, and acknowledg my very greate engagment for the trouble I have, and am like to give you. You desire in your letter a note of what China I would have, wee are already rich enough in Broad Hat China dishes, our designe is for any other fashion to mingle with them, butt beeing nott to bee purchased without difficulty in those parts you are going to, makes us dispaire of itt. Butt if there doe Happen a sale while you are att Lisbon you will oblige mee much if you m ake mee a smale purchase, so far as you beleive my purse (whichis nott a deep one) may bee able to pay you againe, and with that some Portugall ware. My sister is your servant, and will tell you so herselfe when shee is out of the Straw, shee bid mee t ell you the Boy is to hinder her frome nothing shee formerly tooke delight in, and because shee will not bee fond, sends him a -grazing 3 miles of[f] in the Country, and then falls amaine to her Painting. Since you went hence Mr Curten has married Mistris Wood's Neice Nan Drope. Mr An: Wood so highly resents itt, whether for the loss of his bosome friend or for the Lass, I know nott, butt itt has almost Crackt his braine. Mr Ben Parry has gott a very good Parsonage nigh Windsor and is going to live with th e Bishop of Winchester, in hopes of more preferment, the former beeing the Gift of a privat Patron. Had wee knowne your Stay would have been above a Moneth in London, here is a Party of your friends in Oriell College sweare they would have laid violent h ands on you rather than you should have gone so soon. I will detaine you no longer frome whatever this finds you doing, than to wish you a happy and prosperous voyage, and a speedy returne, I am Your faithfull friend and servant AS My Husband presents you with his affectionate service I doe fancy that your Jarrs and Bottles of China may nott bee to[o] deere in Portugall and fine thin dishes. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Anne Say and her sister Sarah Lydall to Francis Parry 3 November 1668 Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford MS. Eng. lett. c. 328, fols 600r –601v (with seal) Nov. the 3d Sir I received your obliging letter so long since that I blush to thinke I have nott been so civill as to answer itt, really the fault is more Mistris Lydall's than mine, I suppose in kindness to you, thinking itt not proper to trouble a person that is imployed in affaires of state with women's impertinent scribles, butt since you are pleased to desire itt, when I have told you I was extreame glad to heare you so well escaped the dangerous storme att Sea, Ile give you such an account as I can of our t owne affaires. Wee have lost our good friend Mr George Moore who died last June in Spaine of a Calenture, there is chose in his place Mr Haselwoods sonne of your College. Mr Whitehall is married and gone with his Miss to his Parsonage in Northamptonshire , and wee heare is made Prebend of Peterborough, butt that which you will beleive dos much afflict mee is the loss of my Cosen Sarah Barry, who this Sommer has made good an old promise and married Mr Gunter, who beeing then Parson of Hampton had the oppert unity of courting and contracted her unknowne to any friend shee had, the most good I can heare is the plenty of the Country hee has carryed her into which hee ill credits, looking more like the Picture of Famine than any thing that good is. I doubt that s hee which was nott contented with her condition in this country, shee will nott long thinke herselfe happy in a Norfolke Vicarage. You may well thinke mee much att a loss, having scarce any of those aquaintance left which you were wont to meett heare, an d I doubt itt will nott bee in the good old President's power to make good his promise to mee of Sitting in the Liberary to heare his favourite preach on Xmas day. His wife is gone to the Wedding of her Nephew who is married to the most famous dauncing Las s in that Country. Dr Hood is dead and Dr Crew Rector, the Vice chancellour continue[s], Mr Hodges of Christ Church has Mr Crisps Lecture, Mistris Baylie is dead and has made her sonne John ('tis beleived very rich by being) her Executor, Mistris Betty is very blight and gone to live with her Sister Dighton. My Master has been much indisposed this Somer, hee has gone through a course of Physick and I thanke God is much recovered. Dr Hurst has made Mistris Hyde a widdow once againe. Dr Thomas thrives amaine att Salisbury, I told him I beleived his practice was most amonge the Maiden Ladys and that his only way to oblige all was to live single. I have nothing to say by way of excuse for this tedious nothing, butt that I thinke your letters goe franck, which I hope may make you the more willing to grant a pardon to Your faithfull friend and servant AS. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Anne Say to Francis Parry 25 July 1669 Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford MS. Eng. lett. c. 328, fols 602r–603v (with seal) Oriell College July 25 / 1669 Sir 'Tis high tyme to tell you that I received your letter att Xmas by the hands of Dr Paris, and would nott have been so long before I had returned my thankes, butt that I waited to heare of Sir Robert Southwell's coming home, because I knew you would nott ha ve an oppertunity of buying for us, till hee had made his Marketts of China. The string you sent tells us you buy greate Bargains att Lisbone, and if itt may nott disparage the grandure that you are now in, to deale for so little as our purses will reach , you will oblige my Sister, and mee, to make us a Purchase as far as 10 Guineys will goe, leaving out flat dishes, wee shall leave the fashion of our China to you, whether Basons or Bottles -- provided itt bee nott all of a sort. Pray putt in a sprinkling of Portugall Plate (as tis called here) if you find you can dispose of this money, for any thing else that you thinke may please us idle folke wee shall leave itt to your discretion who I am sure can make a better choice, than wee can direct, that so seld ome see fine things, and if you doe happen (to bee tempted by a good Bargaine of any thing) to exceed the ten Guineys wee will bee sure to stand to itt, the thing I most feare is paying of Custome, for the bringing over, wee leave that to your managment wh o understand those things. Our great Act has left the towne very full of discourse especially of the two foule mouthed Terifillis, who were abusive beyond any that ever went before them, my good Master was up for company, I thank God I scaped which is mo re than many neighbours of my Sex can say, a Lady in this towne, who I have heard you say was your schoolefellow att Salisbury, was horridly used by them, butt 'tis as unfitt for mee to write as 'twas for them to speake, therefore I begge your pardon for n ott writing perticulars of Oxford affaires because I know nott whose hands my letters may fall into. I wrote to you as I remember in November, I sent itt to Mr Brace, who told mee hee conveyed itt by Mr Ch[arles] Ashburnham, I fancy itt never came to your hands. This Act brought downe the Dukes Players. They Acted 17 playes in the Court to the Guild Hall which they made as hansome as they could with scaffolds, and covering like a tent, the place was far short of a London play house, butt the Acters beeing the same brought so much company to them that[?] they owned the taking of £1550 in the nine dayes, which makes them have so much kindness, for themselves, or Oxford, as to say that if they may have leave they will build themselves a Theater; and come downe every Act, which I beleive will nott bee allowed, for the good of the young schollars, who were so much delighted, that 'twas said to putt some to greate streights for money, even to the powning [ sic] of their Blanketts. Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford Transcription by Bruce Barker -Benfield . Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 Your Countryman Dr Therbury is go ing into Italy upon a very noble employment to bee Governour to the mad Duke of Norfolke, Mr Houghton like a cuning fox went this Act to Salisbury to save charges, hee called going and coming att Tedworth to see your Sisters, hee says they bee very good me rry Girles, and treated him nobly, butt hee scorned to bee obliged by them, and made them a returne of Crafish and such other provant as was in the bottom of his pockett to keep the poore wretch frome starving in the Jorney. Yesterday was a tryall att ou r assizes between the University and towne for Fellons goods, the University had the better to the no smale greife of the towne. I am nott to know that Mr Parry is now a very greate person, and ought nott to bee wrote to att such a rambling rate as I am fa ine to doe, I cannott forgett the freedome you were wont to allow your friends, which gives mee hopes that you may bee inclined to pardon as well the ignorance, as confidence of Sr Your faithfull friend and Servant A.S. My Mother and Husband present their affectionate service to you Alice is your humble servant and desires you to remember: proceed in vertue's trace Address: These / For Mr Francis Parry at Lisbone present Endorsed by Parry: Oxford July 25. 1669 from Mrs Say Received Octob. 4. at Cuitra by a ship from London

Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Anne Say to Francis Parry 10 February 1669/70 Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford MS. Eng. lett. c. 328, fols 604r–605v Sir Though I have little of concern to aquaint you with, I cannot forbeare sometimes to ask you how you doe, to whom I am much obliged by many civilitys both by your selfe and Brother who most kindly gave us a vissit in your name, and engaged mee to convey a letter by him which I intend to doe by the assistance of my good friend Mr Houghton. Wee have lost our old fello[w] Mr Duncomb who has left behind him the most lasting testimony of his affection to his friend that I believe you ever heard of, hee has given £15 to the College to buy a peice of Plate to bee inscribed with M[r] John Heywoods name (who died fellow of this College 7 yeares since). Mr Duncomb could nott prevaile with his Mother to bestow anything to continue the Memory of her Sonne in this place, sure 'twill putt her much out of countenance to heare that a person no wayes related should so much exceed her in kindness to her only child. The Fanaticks were never so ferreted out as by this Vice Chancellor, for which hee has received thanks frome the King and Councill, not long since hee brought some of them to St Marys by head and shoulders. Happy are you that live this Winter in a warme climate, this is thought the severest Winter that ever came in England, and greatest scarcity of watter, there is nott so much watter in our river a s for Boats which goe between this place and London to come any neerer than Wallingford, some times they stope att Henley, and I beleive hardly a pond in these parts which the fish are nott destroyed for want of Watter. Mistris Croudey says very true when shee tells you shee is mighty lazy, shee wants some of her old aquaintance to teaze her out of itt, if they could catch her without a great Belly, she has now the 3d. and as gravely sitts as if shee had a dozen. I must now return my hearty thanks for your ready acceptance of the trouble of biying us some China Ware, and wish itt may ever lye in my power to make a proportionate returne of service, having a very great engagment to desire a power to express myselfe to you Good Mr Francis Feb: the 10th A faithfull and affectionate servant A Say My Mo(ther) and the Pro(vost) present their service to you Address: These To Mr Francis Parry att Lisbone present Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford Transcription by Bruce Barker -Benfield .
